1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. RDS: Relational Database Service; EMR: Elastic MapReduce; MSK: Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka; HNSW: Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds; IVF: inverted file; MPP: massively parallel processing; OLAP: online analytical processing; BI: business intelligence; OSS: open source software; AZ: Availability Zone; RDF: Resource Description Framework; EBS: Elastic Block Store; EFS: Elastic File System; DAX: DynamoDB Accelerator; TTL: time to live; SFTP: Secure File Transfer Protocol; FTPS: File Transfer Protocol Secure; FTP: File Transfer Protocol; AS2: Applicability Statement 2; ETL: extract, transform, load; ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability

  • Match a workload to a store: Redshift, DynamoDB, RDS and Aurora, S3, EMR, Lake Formation, MemoryDB, Neptune, DocumentDB, Keyspaces, OpenSearch, Kinesis and MSK
  • Configure each store for its access pattern, cost and performance
  • Use vector indexes (HNSW, IVF) and MemoryDB for fast lookups and similarity search
  • Integrate migration tools such as AWS Transfer Family
  • Use Redshift federated queries, materialized views and Spectrum for remote access
  • Manage locks and open table formats such as Apache Iceberg

2Matching the Workload to the Store (skills 2.1.1 and 2.1.2)

Running case

Kestrel Freight Picks Its Stores

  • Raw telemetry and files need cheap, durable storage
  • Invoices need relational integrity and joins
  • Live truck status must be read in milliseconds by key
  • Analysts run heavy aggregate reports over years of data
  • Search over delivery notes and a "similar issues" feature
  • Your job: one workload, one store, with the right settings

Store Model and strength Pick it when
Amazon S3 Object storage, 11 nines durability, cheap, any format Data lake, raw and curated zones, archives, files for Athena, EMR, Glue
Amazon Redshift Columnar MPP data warehouse (SQL, OLAP) Heavy analytics and BI over large structured data; joins and aggregates
Amazon DynamoDB Key-value and document, serverless, single-digit millisecond at any scale Known access patterns by key, high write rates, spiky traffic
Amazon RDS / Aurora Relational OLTP (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server; Aurora MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible) Transactions, joins, referential integrity, existing SQL apps
Amazon MemoryDB Durable in-memory database, Valkey and Redis OSS compatible, microsecond reads, single-digit millisecond writes, Multi-AZ transaction log Primary database for ultra-fast key/value, session, leaderboard, vector data; no separate cache needed
Amazon Neptune Graph database (property graph and RDF) Highly connected data: fraud rings, recommendations, knowledge graphs, lineage
Amazon DocumentDB Document database, MongoDB-compatible Existing MongoDB workloads, flexible JSON documents
Amazon Keyspaces Apache Cassandra-compatible, serverless wide-column Existing Cassandra workloads
Amazon OpenSearch Service Search and analytics engine, log analytics, k-NN vector search Full-text search, log and event analysis, semantic search
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams / MSK Streams with retention Replayable event logs (Module 2)
Amazon EMR (HDFS) / EBS / EFS Cluster file system / block / shared file Transient cluster storage; shared files; prefer S3 for durable data
AWS Lake Formation Governed data lake on S3 and the Glue catalog Central permissions and cataloging for the lake (Modules 7 and 15)
Exam tip

The access pattern decides: ad-hoc SQL over huge data → Redshift (or Athena on S3); lookups by key at massive scale → DynamoDB; transactions and joins → RDS or Aurora; cheap durable storage of anything → S3.

Amazon Redshift configuration

  • Provisioned (RA3 nodes with managed storage that separates compute from storage) or Redshift Serverless (scales automatically, pay for use, good for spiky or unpredictable workloads)
  • Distribution style decides how rows spread over slices: AUTO (default, Redshift chooses), EVEN (round robin; no joins or unclear), KEY (same key on the same slice: co-locate joined tables), ALL (a full copy on every node: small, rarely changing dimension tables)
  • Sort keys order rows on disk so range filters skip blocks: compound (leading column first) or AUTO; automatic table optimization can tune them
  • Concurrency scaling and workload management (WLM) keep many users responsive; materialized views speed repeated queries
  • Load with COPY, unload with UNLOAD (Module 8)

Amazon DynamoDB configuration

  • Capacity modes: on-demand (pay per request; unpredictable traffic) or provisioned (set read and write capacity; predictable traffic, with auto scaling)
  • Primary key: a partition key (and optional sort key) that spreads load evenly; avoid a hot partition
  • Secondary indexes: global (GSI) (any key, own capacity, eventually consistent) and local (LSI) (same partition key, different sort key, created with the table)
  • DAX is a managed cache in front of DynamoDB for microsecond reads; TTL, streams and point-in-time recovery (Module 8)

RDS and Aurora configuration

  • Instance class and storage type for the workload; Multi-AZ for high availability; read replicas for read scaling; Aurora shares one cluster volume across up to 15 replicas and offers Aurora Serverless v2
  • Use RDS Proxy to pool connections from Lambda and other bursty clients

Amazon EMR and Lake Formation

  • EMR: use S3 as the durable store and HDFS only for temporary shuffle or hot data; choose instance fleets with Spot
  • Lake Formation adds fine-grained permissions and cataloging to the S3 lake

3Vector Stores, MemoryDB and Index Types (skills 2.1.3 and 2.1.8)

  • A vector is a list of numbers (an embedding) that represents the meaning of text, an image or a record; similar items have nearby vectors
  • A vector store keeps embeddings and finds the nearest neighbors (k-NN) by cosine similarity, Euclidean distance or inner product
  • Where vectors live: Aurora PostgreSQL and RDS for PostgreSQL (the pgvector extension), Amazon OpenSearch Service (k-NN plugin, knn_vector fields), Amazon MemoryDB (vector search in memory), Amazon DocumentDB and Neptune Analytics; knowledge bases for Amazon Bedrock can use Aurora PostgreSQL, OpenSearch and other stores

Index How it works Trade-offs
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds) A layered graph of neighbors; a search hops from a coarse layer down to the nearest points High recall and fast queries, no training step; more memory and slower to build
IVF (inverted file, IVFFlat in pgvector) Vectors are grouped into clusters (centroids); a search checks only the nearest few clusters (probes) Faster to build, less memory; recall depends on the number of clusters and probes; needs data present to build
Exact (no index) Compares every vector Perfect recall, slow for large sets
  • Both are approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes: they trade a little recall (accuracy) for much lower latency
  • pgvector 0.5.0 or later supports HNSW indexes on Aurora PostgreSQL

Amazon MemoryDB for fast key/value access

  • All data in memory, microsecond reads, single-digit millisecond writes, durable across multiple AZs by a transaction log: unlike a cache, it can be the system of record
  • Use for session state, real-time leaderboards, rate limits and low-latency feature or vector lookups
Exam tip

"Similarity search in an existing PostgreSQL database" → Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector and an HNSW index. "Durable microsecond key/value store" → MemoryDB. "Faster index build and lower memory, lower recall acceptable" → IVF.

4Migration Tools and Remote Access (skills 2.1.4 and 2.1.5)

AWS Transfer Family (skill 2.1.4)

  • Managed file transfer into and out of S3 and EFS over SFTP, FTPS, FTP and AS2; no servers to run
  • Use when partners or legacy systems send files by SFTP; files land in S3 and can trigger event-driven ingestion (Module 1)
  • Related tools: AWS DataSync (managed online transfer), AWS DMS (databases), AWS Snow Family (offline), Application Discovery Service and Application Migration Service (servers and applications)

Redshift remote access (skill 2.1.5)

Feature What it does Pick it when
Redshift Spectrum Query files in S3 through external tables (Glue Data Catalog) without loading them; processing happens in the Spectrum layer Cold or huge data stays in S3, joined with warehouse tables
Federated query Query live data in RDS or Aurora (PostgreSQL, MySQL) from Redshift Join operational data with the warehouse without ETL
Materialized view Stores the precomputed result of a query; refresh automatically or manually; can be built over external and streaming sources Repeated expensive queries, dashboards, streaming ingestion
Data sharing Share live data between Redshift clusters or accounts Module 18
COPY / UNLOAD Load from and write to S3 Module 8
Exam tip

"Query historical files in S3 from Redshift without loading them" → Redshift Spectrum. "Join live Aurora data with warehouse tables, no pipeline" → federated query. "Speed up the same heavy dashboard query" → materialized view.

5Locks (skill 2.1.6)

  • A lock stops other sessions from changing (or reading) data while a transaction is using it, so results stay consistent
  • Amazon Redshift: each statement auto-commits unless you use BEGIN/END; readers see the latest committed snapshot and do not wait for writers; concurrent writes to the same table can queue or fail with a serializable isolation error; TRUNCATE and VACUUM commit open transactions; find sessions and locks in system views (for example STV_LOCKS) and end a blocking session (PG_TERMINATE_BACKEND)
  • Amazon RDS and Aurora: the engine uses row and table locks; long transactions hold locks and cause lock waits and deadlocks (the engine rolls back one victim); use short transactions, consistent access order, and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE only where needed
  • Prevent problems: keep transactions short, commit promptly, schedule heavy loads away from reports, and retry after a deadlock or serialization error
  • DynamoDB has no row locks: use conditional writes, transactions and optimistic locking with a version attribute
Exam tip

"A Redshift load blocks other statements" or "deadlock" → find the blocking session in the lock system views, keep transactions short and retry.

6Open Table Formats and Amazon S3 Tables (skill 2.1.7)

  • A table format adds table-level metadata on top of data files in S3 so engines treat them as real tables
  • Apache Iceberg (also Apache Hudi and Delta Lake) gives ACID transactions, schema evolution, partition evolution, time travel (query or roll back to an earlier snapshot), row-level updates and deletes and hidden partitioning
  • Iceberg works with Athena, AWS Glue, Amazon EMR, Amazon Redshift and Apache Spark, with the Glue Data Catalog as the catalog
  • Maintenance for self-managed Iceberg: compact small files, expire old snapshots, remove orphan files
  • Amazon S3 Tables are table buckets that store Apache Iceberg tables natively with automatic compaction, snapshot management and unreferenced-file removal, higher transactions per second than self-managed tables, access control in the s3tables namespace and integration with the Glue Data Catalog; query with Athena, Redshift, EMR, Spark and Quick
Exam tip

"Row-level updates and deletes and time travel on a data lake in S3" → Apache Iceberg. "Iceberg tables without managing compaction" → Amazon S3 Tables.

7Exam Q&A

7.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Kestrel Freight's analysts run complex aggregate queries with joins across five years of structured shipment data and need the best price-performance for repeated BI reports. Which store fits best?

  • AAmazon DynamoDB
  • BAmazon ElastiCache
  • CAmazon Keyspaces
  • DAmazon Redshift
Show the answer

Answer: D. Redshift is a columnar MPP data warehouse built for heavy analytic SQL. DynamoDB is for key-based access and Keyspaces for Cassandra workloads.

S2A truck-status service must read the latest position by truck ID in single-digit milliseconds at very high scale with spiky traffic and no capacity planning. What should the engineer choose?

  • AAmazon DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode
  • BAmazon RDS for MySQL with several read replicas
  • CAmazon Redshift Serverless with a materialized view
  • DAmazon EMR with HDFS on the core nodes
Show the answer

Answer: A. DynamoDB on-demand serves key lookups at low latency and scales with spiky traffic without capacity planning.

S3A team needs similarity search over embeddings stored in an existing Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database, with fast queries and high recall. Which TWO choices apply? (Select TWO.)

  • AUse DISTSTYLE ALL
  • BEnable the pgvector extension
  • CMove the data to Amazon S3 Glacier
  • DUse a DynamoDB global secondary index
  • ECreate an HNSW index on the vector column
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. pgvector adds the vector type and similarity operators, and an HNSW index gives fast approximate nearest-neighbor search with high recall. The other options do not provide vector search.

S4A company stores years of rarely queried files in S3 and wants Redshift users to query them together with warehouse tables without loading them. Which feature should be used?

  • ARedshift federated query
  • BCOPY with a manifest
  • CRedshift Spectrum
  • DRedshift data sharing
Show the answer

Answer: C. Spectrum queries files in S3 through external tables without loading them and can join them with local tables. Federated query is for live RDS or Aurora data.

S5A data lake in S3 needs row-level updates and deletes, schema evolution and the ability to query earlier snapshots. Which approach fits best?

  • APlain CSV files with Athena
  • BApache Iceberg tables
  • CGzip-compressed JSON files
  • DAmazon EBS snapshots
Show the answer

Answer: B. Iceberg adds ACID transactions, row-level changes, schema evolution and time travel on top of files in S3.

S6Which statement about distribution styles in Amazon Redshift is correct?

  • AALL distribution suits small, slowly changing dimension tables that are joined often
  • BKEY distribution keeps a full copy of the table on every node of the cluster for joins
  • CEVEN distribution places matching values on the same slice
  • DAUTO distribution requires you to choose a column
Show the answer

Answer: A. ALL copies the whole table to every node, which suits small slowly changing tables. KEY co-locates matching values, EVEN is round robin, and AUTO lets Redshift choose.

S7A durable, in-memory database is needed as the primary store for session data, with microsecond reads and Multi-AZ durability. Which service should be used?

  • AAmazon MemoryDB
  • BAmazon S3
  • CAmazon Redshift
  • DAmazon DocumentDB
Show the answer

Answer: A. MemoryDB is a durable in-memory database compatible with Valkey and Redis OSS, with microsecond reads and a Multi-AZ transaction log.

S8Partners deliver files by SFTP every day, and the company wants them in S3 without running servers. Which service should be used?

  • AAWS Snow Family
  • BAmazon Kinesis Data Streams
  • CAWS DMS
  • DAWS Transfer Family
Show the answer

Answer: D. Transfer Family provides managed SFTP, FTPS and FTP endpoints that write into S3 or EFS.
